off.text:
From the offline source:
Signs and symptoms: 80% of people who get the dengue virus have no symptoms, or have only mild symptoms (like a basic fever). About 5% of infected people get much sicker. A small number of those infected have symptoms that could kill them. After a person gets the dengue virus from a mosquito, it takes between 3 and 14 days for them to get sick. (This is called the virus's incubation period.) Often, when children have dengue fever, their symptoms are the same as gastroenteritis (stomach flu), like vomiting and diarrhea, or the common cold. Children are more likely to have bad complications from dengue fever. Dengue fever happens in three stages: febrile, critical, and recovery. [5]

Altitude sickness (headache, nausea, dizziness, tiredness at altitude): stop and rest at the same altitude until you feel better; don't go higher, and never go up to sleep higher with symptoms. Don't use alcohol or sleeping pills to help you sleep at altitude. If symptoms get worse or don't improve after a day, go down about 300 to 1,000 metres. Go down straight away and get medical help immediately (call emergency services if you can) if they are confused, unsteady, breathless at rest, coughing up frothy or bloody spit, or very sleepy.

Source: NHS, Altitude sickness; CDC Yellow Book, High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

Jellyfish sting: get out of the water. Don't touch the tentacles with bare hands; remove any with tweezers or the edge of a card. Rinse the sting with seawater, not fresh water. In tropical box-jellyfish areas, pour vinegar on the sting and go to hospital. For pain, soak the area in very warm water, as hot as they can bear without burning, for at least 30 minutes. Don't pee on it and don't put ice on it. Call emergency services if they have trouble breathing, chest pain, a seizure, severe swelling, vomiting, or feel faint.

Source: NHS, Jellyfish and other sea creature stings; healthdirect (AU), Jellyfish stings. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Emergency — Thailand: police 191, ambulance 1669, fire 199, tourist police 1155 (English-speaking).

off.text:
Snakebite, first aid: move away from the snake and don't try to catch or kill it. Call emergency services now; if you are alone, call right away and follow their instructions. Keep the person still and calm, lying down, on their side if possible, and stop them from moving around at all; carry them on a makeshift stretcher if you can, and get them to medical care without delay, for antivenom: don't wait for symptoms. Take off rings, watches and bracelets, and loosen clothing near the bite, before swelling starts. Cover the bite with a clean, dry dressing. Mark the edge of the swelling on the skin and write down the time. Do NOT use a tourniquet, do NOT cut the wound, and do NOT suck the venom or put chemicals on it. Don't put ice on it or soak it in water. Don't drink alcohol, and don't take aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen. If you can do it safely from a distance, take a photo of the snake to help identify it. If the person stops responding or stops breathing normally, start CPR.

Sources: WHO, questions and answers on snakebite envenoming (2019); CDC NIOSH, Venomous Snakes at Work; NHS, Snake bites; healthdirect Australia, Snake bites.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).
